Standish, JPL Solar System Dynamics, "Keplerian Elements for Approximate Positions of the Major Planets", Table 1 (1800 AD - 2050 AD), https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/planets/approx_pos.html (data file https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/txt/p_elem_t1.txt); Earth uses the EM Bary row. sun.name: Sun
facts: Holds about 99.86% of the Solar System's mass.
Its surface is about 5,500 degrees C; the core reaches about 15 million degrees C.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.

planets.name: Mercury
facts: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun.
One solar day lasts about 176 Earth days, twice its year.
Surface temperatures swing from about -180 to 430 degrees C.

planets.name: Venus
facts: The hottest planet, at about 465 degrees C, due to a runaway greenhouse effect.
Rotates backwards (retrograde), and a sidereal day is longer than its year.
Surface pressure is about 92 times Earth's.

planets.name: Earth
facts: The only world known to host life.
About 71% of the surface is covered by oceans.
Its axial tilt of 23.4 degrees causes the seasons.

planets.name: Mars
facts: Home to Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the Solar System.
Its red colour comes from iron oxide dust.
Has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

planets.name: Jupiter
facts: The largest planet: more than twice the mass of all other planets combined.
The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth.
Has the shortest day of any planet, just under 10 hours.

planets.name: Saturn
facts: Its main rings span about 270,000 km but are mostly only tens of metres thick.
Less dense than water on average.
Winds near the equator reach about 1,800 km/h.

planets.name: Uranus
facts: Spins on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees.
An ice giant whose methane atmosphere gives it a blue-green colour.
Each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight, then 42 of darkness.

planets.name: Neptune
facts: The most distant planet, about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth.
Has the fastest winds measured in the Solar System, over 2,000 km/h.
Its existence was predicted mathematically before it was observed in 1846.
